name: Khan Academy Kids
origin_region: Global (built by Khan Academy, a US non-profit based in Mountain View, California; distributed worldwide via iOS/Android app stores including Indonesia)
target_age: Ages 2-8, i.e. PreK through 2nd grade. Common Sense Media notes the content mainly stretches up to 1st grade, with some math and ELA lessons for 2nd graders.
delivery_mode: online-app (tablet/phone app for iOS and Android, plus a limited web presence). No genuine offline mode - offline use has been a long-standing open user request in the Khan Academy help community, so an unreliable or shared-device / low-data household is a real constraint.
language_localization: English only. Khan Academy's help center states the Kids app is still available only in English with no timeline for translation, even though the main khanacademy.org platform IS localized into Bahasa Indonesia. So: zero Bahasa Indonesia in the child UI, in the audio narration, or in parent-facing progress views. [uncertain] whether any partial Spanish build has shipped since 2025.
pricing_model: free - '100% free, forever', no ads, no subscriptions, no in-app purchases. Funded as a non-profit. This makes it the price floor any Indonesian paid product must justify itself against.
local_curriculum_alignment: No alignment with Kurikulum Merdeka or K13. Content is designed against US early-childhood frameworks (Common Core State Standards and Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework) and is US-context in its examples, names, and cultural references. [uncertain] exact framework list, as Khan Academy documents this only loosely on public pages.
does_error_type_diagnosis: no. Khan Academy Kids tracks WHETHER a skill is mastered, never WHY a child got something wrong. The app's entire feedback surface is a three-state mastery flag per activity (mastered / in progress / developing) plus an automatic difficulty adjustment of the learning path. There is no classification of reading errors vs conceptual misconceptions vs arithmetic slips, no distractor-to-misconception mapping exposed to anyone, and no error-type label anywhere in the parent view.
diagnosis_granularity: topic-mastery-map. The 'All Progress' report lists every lesson completed and shows fractions of skills mastered; in the Library each completed activity carries a colored checkmark - green for mastered, yellow for in progress, red for developing. That is a per-activity mastery state map, one level coarser than even a trouble-spot-quantity signal: there is no count of which item types a child repeatedly misses, and certainly no error taxonomy.
diagnosis_input_modality: mcq-distractor and touch-interaction only. Children answer by tapping a choice, dragging objects, or tracing letters; the microphone is used for some literacy/reading activities. Math answers are effectively selected-response or manipulated-object response. There is no free-response OCR of a child's written work, no pen-stroke/working-out capture for math, and no video or self-report channel through which a child could show HOW they solved something. [uncertain] whether newer number-writing activities capture and score stroke data - tracing exists for letters, but no evidence it is analyzed diagnostically.
ai_tutor_diagnosis_reliability: Not applicable - there is no AI diagnosis component to validate, so there is also no known failure mode such as the 'correct answer trap'. Khanmigo, Khan Academy's LLM tutor, is a SEPARATE paid product and is not embedded in the Kids app: it requires an account holder who is 18+, US-resident with a US billing address, who then enables access for up to 10 children; its learner-facing tutoring is oriented at roughly grades 4-10 (the writing tutor is documented for grades 4-10). The result is a structural gap: the 2-8 age band that Khan Academy serves for free is precisely the band with NO AI tutor and NO error-type diagnosis.
evidence_quote: Khan Academy help documentation on Kids progress reports: 'each activity that a child has completed will have a colored checkmark on the activity icon (green for mastered, yellow for in progress, and red for developing)' and the All Progress report 'shows every lesson that students have completed and displays fractions showing how many skills have been mastered.' Common Sense Media's review adds that 'activities are automatically presented according to age and past performance' and that 'there's some limited feedback to track progress, but not so much as to feel overwhelming.' Every one of these is a mastery/quantity signal; none names a kind of error.
how_parent_involved: gatekeeper + dashboard-only. The parent is a gatekeeper at setup (an email address must be supplied and confirmed, child profiles are created by the adult, microphone permission must be granted) and thereafter a passive dashboard viewer: the 'For Parents' / Grown-Up section is behind a swipe gate and offers completed-activity lists, mastery checkmarks, assignable activities, and time limits. Crucially, the dashboard tells a parent that a child is 'developing' on a skill but gives the parent nothing to SAY or DO about the specific mistake - no explanation script, no 'your child is confusing X with Y', no coaching prompt. For a low-math-confidence Indonesian parent this dashboard is effectively unactionable.
ai_tutor_directly_to_child: no. There is no conversational AI in the Khan Academy Kids app. Guidance is delivered by five scripted, pre-recorded characters (narrator Kodi Bear and friends) - fixed audio, not generated dialogue, and not responsive to what the child specifically got wrong. Khanmigo, which does chat directly with a learner, is gated behind an 18+ paying US account and is not offered inside the Kids age band.
key_finding: Khan Academy Kids is the strongest possible 'free baseline' competitor - genuinely free forever, no ads, mastery-based, award-winning, with independent RCT evidence - and yet it does NOT do error-type diagnosis at all, and it has NO AI tutor speaking to the child. It is a two-signal product: mastered / not-yet-mastered, plus an auto-adjusting difficulty path. This defines the gap precisely: the market's most credible free early-years product answers 'has my child mastered this?' but never 'what kind of mistake is my child making, and what do I say to fix it?'. Three further gaps compound in the Indonesian context: (1) English-only child UI and audio, with no Bahasa Indonesia despite the main Khan Academy site being localized; (2) no offline mode, which is punishing on a borrowed Android phone with intermittent data; (3) US framework alignment with zero mapping to Kurikulum Merdeka. Notably, Khan Academy's own AI tutor Khanmigo deliberately starts ABOVE this age band - the youngest learners are the segment even the best-funded global non-profit has left without conversational diagnostic support.
study_scale_or_sample: Product-specific efficacy: a randomized controlled trial at the University of Massachusetts Amherst with 49 four- and five-year-olds over 10 weeks, using the Test of Preschool Early Literacy (TOPEL); children were randomly assigned to Khan Academy Kids at home versus age-appropriate non-literacy apps. Result: overall scores rose from the 34th to the 47th percentile, effect size approximately 0.72, versus almost no change in the comparison group. Note the domain: this is PRE-LITERACY, not mathematics. Separately, for the main (non-Kids) Khan Academy platform, a University of Toronto RCT with roughly 11,000 students in grades 3-8 found year-long mastery-learning use improved end-of-year math scores by 0.12 to 0.22 standard deviations.
evidence_strength: moderate. The claims about the absence of error-type diagnosis and the absence of an in-app AI tutor rest on official Khan Academy help documentation plus an independent Common Sense Media review, which is solid. The efficacy claim is weaker than it looks for our purposes: n=49 is small, the outcome was literacy rather than math, and the study is publicized by Khan Academy itself.
remediation_efficacy_evidence: Partial and off-target. There IS randomized evidence that using the product improves outcomes (UMass Amherst RCT, d approx. 0.72, pre-literacy, n=49; and 0.12-0.22 SD in math for the separate main platform in an 11,000-student University of Toronto RCT). But there is NO evidence at all that error-type diagnosis drives remediation, for the simple reason that the product performs no error-type diagnosis - the tested mechanism is mastery-based sequencing and repeated exposure, not identification and targeting of a specific misconception. Nobody in this product line has demonstrated that telling a parent WHICH kind of mistake a child made improves learning.
